title: CSCI 2122 · C Recall and Quiz Practice
description: Self-contained C practice: recall one fact, reconstruct syntax, trace interacting expressions, then write a complete small function from its contract. Commit an answer before revealing the model. A hint-assisted answer means the skill needs another independent attempt.
assumptions: C17 practice model: 8-bit bytes; 32-bit int and unsigned int; sizeof(int) = 4; two’s-complement signed integers; long long can represent 2^31.
Unless a question tests failure or bounds, its pointers and buffers are valid, requested fields fit, numeric input is representable, and operations explicitly stated to succeed do succeed.

Relevant standard headers are included. Size and position calculations are representable unless the question asks you to check them. Any bit-reading convention or helper behavior needed for an answer is stated in that question.

sources.title: C17 language and standard-library rules
sources.detail: Reference: WG14 N1570, a public C draft whose relevant array, pointer, expression, formatted-I/O and allocation rules are unchanged in C17. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

sources.title: Self-contained exercise contracts
sources.detail: Each question gives its needed declarations, values, bit numbering, widths and function contracts. Evaluate the C shown or implement the stated function; no outside input format needs to be recalled.

topics.title: 01 · Binary, hexadecimal and unsigned values
topics.description: Recall number representations, integer division and unsigned conversions.
notes: One hexadecimal digit represents four bits. A hexadecimal literal uses the prefix 0x.
For an unsigned value with w bits, the range is 0 through 2^w − 1; arithmetic and conversions to unsigned use that modulus.
Integer division and remainder split a nonnegative index into a group number and an offset.

topics.title: 02 · Exact input and output syntax
topics.description: Retrieve conversion tokens, destination types, addresses and argument order.
notes: scanf("%d", &count) needs int *; scanf("%x", &temp) needs unsigned int *.
Check how many scanf conversions succeeded before using the destination values.
printf receives values in conversion order; scanf receives destination addresses.

topics.title: 03 · Arrays and pointer layers
topics.description: Distinguish an element, its pointer and the address of that pointer.
notes: p, *p and &p have different types and meanings.
Array objects cannot be assigned, but their elements can. Pointer assignment copies an address value.
sizeof a real array measures the whole array; an array function parameter is adjusted to a pointer. Pass the length separately.

topics.title: 04 · Allocation, byte counts and initialization
topics.description: Separate element count, element size, capacity, valid input and initialization.
notes: calloc(count, size) allocates count × size bytes and initializes their bits to zero; malloc does not initialize storage.
memset writes a byte value into a given number of bytes. Initialization does not make an out-of-bounds access valid.
Allocated capacity and the number of valid input bytes are separate quantities. Check allocation success before use and free dynamic storage when finished.

topics.title: 05 · Masks and bit operators
topics.description: Recall setting, clearing, toggling and isolating selected bits.
notes: Number bits from zero at the least significant bit when building numeric masks.
1u << k selects bit k when k is within the unsigned-int width.
Use OR to set, AND with an inverted mask to clear, and XOR to toggle. Bitwise & differs from logical &&.

topics.title: 06 · Shifts, promotions and undefined behavior
topics.description: Predict values precisely and recognize invalid operations.
notes: A shift count must be nonnegative and smaller than the promoted left operand’s width.
Signed and unsigned shifts have different representability rules; signed 32-bit 1 << 31 is undefined.
unsigned char promotes to nonnegative int in this practice model; plain char may be signed.

topics.title: 07 · Indexing bits inside byte arrays
topics.description: Translate a stated numbering convention into a byte index and shift.
notes: With eight-bit bytes, p / 8 selects the byte and p % 8 gives its within-byte offset.
The prompt specifies whether offsets begin at the MSB or LSB. For MSB-first numbering, the right shift is 7 − p % 8.
An array of count eight-bit bytes has 8 × count bits; zero-based valid positions end one before that total.

topics.title: 08 · Accumulation and changing positions
topics.description: Build values from bits and update cursors according to explicit widths.
notes: Start at zero and append a bit with value = (value << 1) | bit.
An extraction may cross byte boundaries; the question supplies the ordering and selected range.
Advance a cursor by the number of positions actually consumed. Do not assume extra alignment or hidden increments.

topics.title: 09 · Two’s complement at a given width
topics.description: Separate the raw unsigned pattern from its signed interpretation.
notes: For an L-bit two’s-complement value, bit L − 1 carries the sign when numbered from the LSB.
A clear sign bit means the value is raw, including zero. A set sign bit means raw − 2^L.
Compute the negative case in a sufficiently wide signed type, such as (int)((long long)raw - (1LL << L)) for 1 <= L <= 31.

topics.title: 10 · Bounds, loops and counters
topics.description: Trace explicit conditions, cursor changes, break order and variable scope.
notes: Before computing total − pos with size_t, establish pos <= total.
Compare a requested width against total − pos to avoid overflowing pos + width.
A counter initialized inside a loop resets each iteration; statement order around break changes which work is counted.

topics.title: 11 · Combine C concepts
topics.description: Trace complete code that mixes pointers, masks, signed values and lengths.
notes: Track types and values separately at each step.
Evaluate extraction before interpreting its signed value; use the width stated by the code.
A complete code snippet supplies its own operations. No external file layout or output convention needs to be remembered.

topics.title: 12 · Write whole functions from memory
topics.description: Implement small C functions from complete, self-contained contracts.
notes: Read the parameters, result and failure behavior before writing the body. Every exercise supplies its bit order and any helper contracts it uses.
Use local temporary state until validation is complete when failure must leave output arguments unchanged.
Self-check against every rubric point, including boundary values and defined arithmetic.

questions.prompt: What decimal integer is represented by the C literal `0x2a`?
questions.hint: Hexadecimal places have weights 16 and 1.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: What decimal integer is represented by the C literal `0xa5`?
questions.hint: The digit a has value ten.
questions.explanation: The two hexadecimal digits give 10 × 16 + 5 = 165.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: Interpret the bit pattern 101101 as an unsigned binary integer. What is its decimal value?
questions.hint: Add the powers of two at its set bits.
questions.explanation: 101101 is 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45. Leading zeros, if any, would not change its unsigned value.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: Interpret the bit pattern 00001111 as an unsigned binary integer. What is its decimal value?
questions.hint: Only the four low bits are set.
questions.explanation: The value is 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15. The high zero bits contribute nothing.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: How many binary bits are needed to represent one hexadecimal digit?
questions.hint: One hexadecimal digit has sixteen possible values.
questions.explanation: Four bits give 2^4 = 16 possible patterns, matching hexadecimal digits 0 through f.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: How many binary bits are represented by the two hexadecimal digits in `0xff`?
questions.hint: Each hexadecimal digit represents four bits.
questions.explanation: Two digits represent 2 × 4 = 8 bits; ff is the bit pattern 11111111.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: For an unsigned integer with exactly eight value bits, what is the largest representable value?
questions.hint: Set all eight bits to one.
questions.explanation: The range is 0 through 2^8 − 1, so the maximum is 255.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: What decimal value does byte receive when unsigned char has eight value bits?
questions.hint: Conversion to an unsigned integer type reduces the value modulo one more than its maximum.
questions.explanation: The result is 300 modulo 256 = 44. An explicit cast would give the same result; it does not prevent truncation.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.
questions.code: unsigned char byte = 300u;

questions.prompt: What is the value of the C integer expression `13 / 5`?
questions.hint: Both operands have integer type.
questions.explanation: Integer division discards the fractional part; 13 / 5 is 2, not 2.6.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: What is the value of the C integer expression `13 % 5`?
questions.hint: Find what is left after two groups of five.
questions.explanation: 13 = 2 × 5 + 3, so the remainder is 3. This relationship is useful for translating an index into groups and an offset.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: With 32-bit unsigned int, what decimal value is stored in x?
questions.hint: Converting −1 to unsigned wraps modulo 2^32.
questions.explanation: The result is UINT_MAX = 2^32 − 1. Conversion to unsigned is defined modulo the unsigned range, unlike an out-of-range conversion to a signed type.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.
questions.code: unsigned int x = -1;

questions.prompt: With 32-bit unsigned int, what decimal value does x have afterward?
questions.hint: Unsigned arithmetic is reduced modulo 2^32.
questions.explanation: Adding one to the maximum unsigned int wraps to zero. This unsigned addition is defined.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.
questions.code:
unsigned int x = 4294967295u;
x += 1u;

questions.prompt: Fill the format token to read one decimal value into `int count`: `scanf("___", &count);`
questions.hint: The destination is an int, and the input is decimal.
questions.explanation: scanf %d expects a pointer to int, so &count is the correct destination argument.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: Which scanf conversion token reads decimal text into the variable `int length` when passed `&length`?
questions.hint: Use the signed decimal integer conversion.
questions.explanation: The signed decimal integer conversion is %d. Its corresponding destination argument must be int *.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: Fill the format token: `unsigned int temp; scanf("___", &temp);` reads a hexadecimal byte token such as `0xca`.
questions.hint: Hexadecimal without a length modifier.
questions.explanation: scanf %x reads a hexadecimal integer into unsigned int *. It accepts the optional 0x prefix.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: A token is `ff` rather than `0xff`. Which scanf conversion reads it as hexadecimal into unsigned int?
questions.hint: The 0x prefix is optional for this conversion.
questions.explanation: %x accepts both forms. The conversion and destination type must agree.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: With the unmodified `%x` conversion, what exact C type must `temp` have in `scanf("%x", &temp)`?
questions.hint: Do not confuse a byte’s value range with scanf’s destination type.
questions.explanation: Unmodified %x requires unsigned int *. &temp has that type when temp is unsigned int.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: Repair this read while keeping `%x` and the unsigned-char buffer. Assume the token is in 0..255.
questions.hint: Read using the required destination type, then store the byte.
questions.explanation: Passing unsigned char * to unmodified %x is a type mismatch; a cast of that pointer is not a repair. An unsigned-int temporary provides the required object.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
rubric: Reads with unsigned int temp and &temp.
Checks the conversion result before using temp.
Stores temp into data[i] after a successful read.

questions.prompt: Why does reading `int count` use `scanf("%d", &count)` while printing it uses `printf("%d", count)`?
questions.answer: scanf needs count’s address to store a new int in count; printf needs the int value to display.
questions.hint: One operation writes into an object; the other consumes its value.
questions.explanation: C passes each argument by value. For scanf that value is a pointer; for printf %d it is an int.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
rubric: Explains that scanf receives a destination address.
Explains that printf %d receives the integer value.

questions.prompt: Identify and fix the wrong argument in each line.
questions.hint: Match each conversion’s expected argument type.
questions.explanation: scanf %d expects int *, while printf %d expects int. Swapping values and addresses violates those contracts.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
rubric: Adds & for scanf.
Removes & for printf.

questions.prompt: Given `unsigned int temp`, what return value from `scanf("%x", &temp)` means its one requested conversion succeeded?
questions.hint: scanf counts successful assignments.
questions.explanation: One successful conversion gives 1. Do not use temp unless that read succeeded.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: Given `int count` and `unsigned int temp`, `scanf("%d %x", &count, &temp)` assigns count but then fails to convert the second token. What does it return?
questions.hint: Count assignments actually completed.
questions.explanation: The first conversion assigned one object; the second failed, so the return value is 1. EOF before any conversion is a different case.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.

questions.prompt: Write one printf call using `int row`, `int item`, and `int value`. Its output must follow the template `Row <row>, item <item>: <value>` and end with a newline. For row=2, item=4, value=-7, print `Row 2, item 4: -7`.
questions.hint: Place one %d at each integer position in the given template, then pass arguments in matching order.
questions.explanation: Each %d consumes the next int argument. A newline is represented by \n inside the C string literal.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
rubric: Matches the explicitly supplied words, punctuation and spacing.
Uses %d conversions with row, item, value in the matching order.
Ends the printed line with \n.

questions.prompt: What exact output line does this call produce?
questions.hint: Match conversions to arguments from left to right.
questions.explanation: The first argument after the format fills the first %d; variable names do not change that rule.
questions.source: C17 formatted input/output; WG14 N1570 §§7.21.6.1–7.21.6.2.
questions.code:
int row = 4, item = 2, value = -7;
printf("Row %d, item %d: %d\n", item, row, value);
rubric: Gives Row 2, item 4: -7 with the shown punctuation.

questions.prompt: Given `unsigned char *p`, what is the type of the expression `*p`?
questions.hint: One dereference removes one pointer layer.
questions.explanation: p is a pointer to unsigned char; *p designates the unsigned-char object to which it points.

questions.prompt: Given `unsigned char *p`, what is the type of the expression `&p`?
questions.hint: Address-of adds a pointer layer to the variable’s own type.
questions.explanation: p is itself a pointer object. &p points to that pointer object, so its type is unsigned char **.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in x after these statements?
questions.hint: &data[1] points to the second element; * reads that element.
questions.explanation: data[1] is 0xca, which is 202. Dereferencing p reads the pointed-to byte.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in data[0] after these statements?
questions.hint: Two dereferences reach the byte through the pointer object.
questions.explanation: pp points to p; *pp is p; **pp designates data[0]. The assignment therefore writes 8 into that byte.

questions.prompt: Which assignments are valid C, and what does each valid one change?
questions.answer: p = other is valid and redirects p. data[0] = 7 is valid and changes one byte. data = other is invalid because an array is not an assignable object.
questions.hint: Separate an array object, a pointer variable and one array element.
questions.explanation: In most expressions the array name converts to a pointer to its first element, but the array itself cannot be assigned another array or pointer.
rubric: Accepts p = other.
Accepts data[0] = 7.
Rejects data = other rather than claiming it copies bytes.

questions.prompt: Does `p = data` copy five bytes? Explain what it stores.
questions.answer: No. It stores the address of data[0] in p; p then refers to the same array storage.
questions.hint: Pointer assignment copies an address value.
questions.explanation: No new array is created and no elements are copied. Writing p[0] subsequently changes data[0] while p points there.
rubric: Says no element copy occurs.
Identifies the address of the first array element.

questions.prompt: What decimal value does `sizeof data` have here?
questions.hint: sizeof measures bytes of the actual array object.
questions.explanation: An unsigned char occupies one C byte. This real array has five such elements.
questions.code: unsigned char data[5];

questions.prompt: What is `sizeof values / sizeof values[0]` here?
questions.hint: Total array bytes divided by one element’s bytes.
questions.explanation: The expression is the element count, 6. Under the practice assumptions sizeof values is 24, not 6.
questions.code: int values[6];

questions.prompt: Inside this function, does `sizeof data` measure five bytes of array storage? State what it measures.
questions.answer: No. An array parameter is adjusted to a pointer parameter, so sizeof data is sizeof(unsigned char *).
questions.hint: The brackets in a parameter declaration do not preserve an array object.
questions.explanation: Pass the byte count separately. The parameter’s sizeof cannot recover the caller’s array length; pointer size is not assumed here.
rubric: Identifies data as a pointer parameter.
Says sizeof measures the pointer, not the supplied array length.

questions.prompt: Why can this function not obtain the caller’s array length with sizeof data? Give a function signature that supplies the missing byte count.
questions.answer: data is a pointer parameter, so sizeof data is pointer size. Pass the count explicitly, for example void inspect(const unsigned char *data, size_t count).
questions.hint: An array argument does not carry its length into the function.
questions.explanation: The caller must provide the element count separately. Here the elements are unsigned char, so the element count also equals the byte count.
rubric: Rejects sizeof data as the buffer length.
Supplies an explicit length/count parameter.

questions.prompt: After the call, where does caller p point, and what are data[0] and data[1]?
questions.answer: p still points to data[0]; data[0] is 0 and data[1] is 7.
questions.hint: The function receives a copy of the pointer, but both copies refer to shared storage.
questions.explanation: Incrementing local p does not change the caller’s pointer. Dereferencing that local pointer after incrementing changes the second byte.
rubric: Caller p still points to data[0].
Gives data[0] = 0 and data[1] = 7.

questions.prompt: After this call, where does caller p point? Explain the pointer layers.
questions.answer: p points to data[1]. pp points to the caller’s pointer object; *pp is that pointer, so incrementing *pp updates caller p.
questions.hint: This time the function receives the address of the pointer variable.
questions.explanation: A pointer-to-pointer can change which byte the caller’s pointer refers to. No byte value is modified by this increment.
rubric: Identifies data[1] as the new target.
Explains that *pp designates the caller’s pointer.

questions.prompt: `calloc(4, 2)` succeeds. How many total bytes are allocated?
questions.hint: First argument counts elements; second gives bytes per element.
questions.explanation: calloc allocates 4 elements of 2 bytes each: 4 × 2 = 8 bytes. It does not attach an array length to the returned pointer.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.

questions.prompt: In `calloc(4, 2)`, which argument is the element count? Answer its numeric value.
questions.hint: Read the signature as calloc(count, element_size).
questions.explanation: The count argument is 4 and the element-size argument is 2 bytes. Swapping them happens to preserve this product but changes their roles.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.

questions.prompt: The call succeeds. How many int objects fit in this allocation under the practice assumptions?
questions.hint: Divide allocated bytes by sizeof(int).
questions.explanation: calloc(4, 2) reserves 8 bytes, and each int occupies 4 bytes here. The call’s count of 4 does not make it room for four int objects.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
questions.code: int *p = calloc(4, 2);

questions.prompt: The call succeeds. How many total bytes does it reserve under the practice assumptions?
questions.hint: sizeof *p measures one int object.
questions.explanation: The idiom allocates six objects of the pointed-to type: 6 × 4 = 24 bytes.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
questions.code: int *p = calloc(6, sizeof *p);

questions.prompt: Which function guarantees its successfully allocated bytes are initially all-bits-zero: malloc or calloc?
questions.hint: The allocation and initialization contracts differ.
questions.explanation: calloc initializes all allocated bits to zero. For unsigned char bytes that gives the numeric value zero.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.

questions.prompt: A successful `malloc(count)` returns storage for count bytes. May code assume that its unwritten bytes contain zero? Explain.
questions.answer: No. malloc does not initialize the allocated storage. Write byte values before relying on their contents, and stay within the allocated bounds.
questions.hint: Getting storage and setting its contents are separate actions.
questions.explanation: Getting storage and initializing it are separate operations. Neither allocation nor zero-filling confirms that a later input conversion succeeds.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
rubric: Says malloc does not zero the storage.
Requires initialization before using byte values.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does this call write?
questions.hint: The third argument is a byte count.
questions.explanation: memset writes exactly the first 3 bytes here, not all 5 elements of the array.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
questions.code:
unsigned char data[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
memset(data, 0, 3);

questions.prompt: What decimal value is in data[3] afterward?
questions.hint: Indices 0, 1 and 2 are the only bytes filled.
questions.explanation: The byte at index 3 is outside the three-byte fill and keeps its original value 4.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
questions.code:
unsigned char data[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
memset(data, 0, 3);

questions.prompt: Does zeroing a five-byte array make reading data[5] safe? Explain.
questions.answer: No. Valid element indices are 0 through 4; data[5] is outside the array regardless of its initialization.
questions.hint: Initialization changes values, not object boundaries.
questions.explanation: Bounds must be checked against the actual buffer and received stream length. memset does not enlarge either.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.
rubric: Rejects reading data[5].
States the valid indices and separates bounds from initialization.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in data[0] after both statements?
questions.hint: The later assignment replaces the earlier byte value.
questions.explanation: memset first writes zero. The assignment then writes 0x0f, which is 15. Earlier zero-filling does not remove any bits from a later stored value.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and byte filling; WG14 N1570 §§7.22.3, 7.24.6.1.

questions.prompt: p holds the non-null address returned by malloc and has not been freed. Which standard-library function releases that allocation? Give the function name.
questions.hint: Releasing allocated storage is separate from assigning a new value to the pointer variable.
questions.explanation: free(p) releases the allocated storage. The pointer object p is not automatically changed to NULL, and the released storage must not be accessed through it.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and deallocation; WG14 N1570 §7.22.3.

questions.prompt: Write one statement assigning a malloc result to int *p so it can hold count int objects. count is a positive size_t and count <= SIZE_MAX / sizeof *p. Use sizeof *p rather than a hard-coded byte size.
questions.hint: malloc takes one total byte count, unlike calloc’s two arguments.
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of objects by the size of one pointed-to object. The supplied bound ensures that multiplication is representable. In C, assigning malloc’s void * result to int * does not require a cast; check the result before dereferencing it.
rubric: Multiplies count by sizeof *p.
Passes that total byte count as malloc’s single argument.
Assigns the result to p; a cast is optional in C.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and deallocation; WG14 N1570 §7.22.3.

questions.prompt: In an int-returning function, p has just received malloc’s result for a positive requested size. Write a check that returns -1 on allocation failure before any access through p.
questions.hint: malloc reports failure with a null pointer.
questions.explanation: A null result supplies no allocated object to access. The equivalent condition if (!p) is valid. A non-null result can be used only within the requested allocation bounds.
rubric: Tests whether p is null, using p == NULL or !p.
Returns -1 on that path before dereferencing p.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and deallocation; WG14 N1570 §7.22.3.

questions.prompt: Classify the C call `free(NULL)`. Answer defined or undefined.
questions.hint: The deallocation function explicitly handles a null pointer.
questions.explanation: free(NULL) is defined and has no effect. This differs from freeing the same non-null allocation twice or freeing a pointer that was not returned by an allocation function.
questions.source: C17 storage allocation and deallocation; WG14 N1570 §7.22.3.

questions.prompt: Which single C operator performs bit-by-bit AND: & or &&?
questions.hint: One combines bit positions; the other tests truth.
questions.explanation: & keeps a bit set only where both operands have that bit set. && instead returns 0 or 1 from the operands’ truth values.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: What decimal value does x receive?
questions.hint: Compare the one-bits at corresponding positions.
questions.explanation: 2u is binary 10 and 1u is binary 01, so their bitwise AND is 00. Using && here would instead produce 1.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
questions.code: unsigned int x = 2u & 1u;

questions.prompt: Write an unsigned expression with exactly bit k set, where 0 <= k < 32 and bit 0 is the least significant bit.
questions.hint: Start with one at bit 0 and move it k places.
questions.explanation: The u suffix makes the left operand unsigned int. The stated shift-count range avoids an invalid shift.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
rubric: Uses a value with exactly one initial set bit.
Shifts it left by k using an unsigned operand.

questions.prompt: What is the decimal value of the mask `1u << 5`?
questions.hint: Bit k has weight 2^k.
questions.explanation: Moving the unsigned one five places left yields binary 100000, which is 32.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Write a statement that sets bit k of unsigned int x to 1 and preserves all other bits. Assume 0 <= k < 32. Number bits from zero at the least significant bit.
questions.hint: OR with a mask whose only one-bit is at k.
questions.explanation: OR with 1 sets that bit; OR with 0 leaves every other bit unchanged.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
rubric: Builds an unsigned one-bit mask at k.
Uses OR, preserving all other bits.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in x after the operation?
questions.hint: Only bit 1 is forced to one.
questions.explanation: 8u is 1000; the mask is 0010. Their OR is 1010, or 10.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
questions.code:
unsigned int x = 8u;
x |= 1u << 1;

questions.prompt: Write a statement that clears bit k of unsigned int x and preserves all other bits. Assume 0 <= k < 32. Number bits from zero at the least significant bit.
questions.hint: Invert a one-bit mask, then combine with AND.
questions.explanation: The inverted mask has a zero at k and ones elsewhere. AND clears only the selected bit.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
rubric: Uses an inverted unsigned one-bit mask.
Uses AND to preserve all other bits.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in x afterward?
questions.hint: 15 is binary 1111; clear the bit of weight 4.
questions.explanation: The mask clears bit 2, turning 1111 into 1011, which is 11.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
questions.code:
unsigned int x = 15u;
x &= ~(1u << 2);

questions.prompt: Write a statement that toggles bit k of unsigned int x while preserving the others. Assume 0 <= k < 32. Number bits from zero at the least significant bit.
questions.hint: XOR with one flips a bit.
questions.explanation: XOR with the one-bit mask flips bit k; XOR with zero leaves the remaining bits unchanged.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
rubric: Uses XOR.
Applies an unsigned mask containing only bit k.

questions.prompt: What decimal value does x have after both statements?
questions.hint: Toggling the same bit twice restores it.
questions.explanation: The first XOR flips bit 1 off; the second flips it back on. The final value equals the original 10.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is `40u >> 3`?
questions.hint: Unsigned right shift divides by powers of two, discarding low bits.
questions.explanation: 40 divided by 8 is 5. For unsigned values, right shift introduces zeros on the left.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is `43u >> 3`?
questions.hint: Discard the low three bits.
questions.explanation: 43 / 8 has integer quotient 5. The three low bits do not round the result upward.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is `3u << 2`?
questions.hint: Two left shifts multiply this value by four.
questions.explanation: Binary 0011 becomes 1100. No high bits are lost in this example.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is `0x80000000u << 1` under the practice assumptions?
questions.hint: Unsigned results wrap modulo 2^32.
questions.explanation: The only set bit moves beyond the 32-bit unsigned width and is discarded. This unsigned operation is defined.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Classify `1u << 32` with a 32-bit unsigned int. Answer defined or undefined.
questions.hint: A shift count must be smaller than the promoted left operand’s width.
questions.explanation: A count equal to 32 is invalid for a 32-bit operand. Unsigned arithmetic does not make an out-of-range shift count valid.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Classify `1u >> -1`. Answer defined or undefined.
questions.hint: Check the shift count before the direction.
questions.explanation: A negative shift count causes undefined behavior, including for unsigned operands.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Classify `1 << 31` when int is 32 bits. Answer defined or undefined.
questions.hint: The literal 1 has type int, not unsigned int.
questions.explanation: The mathematical result 2^31 is not representable in signed 32-bit int. Use an appropriate unsigned or wider signed operand for the intended operation.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Which suffix makes the left operand unsigned int in `1___ << 31`? Give just the suffix.
questions.hint: The fix is a type choice, not parentheses.
questions.explanation: 1u is unsigned int, making this 31-place shift valid under the 32-bit unsigned assumptions. This does not by itself make unsigned subtraction a signed-decoding formula.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: In `data[i] >> shift`, data[i] is a valid unsigned-char array element and shift is an int in 0..7. Is the promoted value of data[i] ever negative under the practice assumptions? Explain.
questions.answer: No. unsigned char values are 0..255, all representable in 32-bit int, so promotion to int preserves a nonnegative value.
questions.hint: Small integer operands undergo integer promotion before shifting.
questions.explanation: Using unsigned-char storage avoids signed-char negative byte values. Right shift of these promoted nonnegative values has the intended bit-extraction result.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
rubric: States the 0..255 range.
Explains promotion to int preserves that nonnegative value.

questions.prompt: Why is unsigned char useful for bytes that will be right-shifted, compared with plain char?
questions.answer: unsigned char guarantees nonnegative byte values. Plain char may be signed, so a byte with its top bit set can promote to a negative int.
questions.hint: The signedness of plain char is implementation-defined.
questions.explanation: Under the practice model unsigned-char values are 0..255 and promote to nonnegative int. In C17, right-shifting a negative signed value is implementation-defined.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
rubric: Identifies plain char’s possible signedness.
Connects unsigned-char values to predictable nonnegative shift operands.

questions.prompt: Number the eight bits of data[0] from its MSB to its LSB, then continue the same way through data[1], data[2], and so on, beginning at global position 0. At global stream bit position p = 19, what byte index contains the bit?
questions.hint: Each byte holds eight consecutive stream positions.
questions.explanation: Integer division gives 19 / 8 = 2. The valid positions in byte 2 are 16 through 23.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Number the eight bits of data[0] from its MSB to its LSB, then continue the same way through data[1], data[2], and so on, beginning at global position 0. A bit is at global position p = 8. What is its byte index?
questions.hint: The first byte ends at global position 7.
questions.explanation: 8 / 8 = 1: position 8 is the first bit of the second byte, not another bit of byte 0.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Number the eight bits of data[0] from its MSB to its LSB, then continue the same way through data[1], data[2], and so on, beginning at global position 0. For p = 19, how many positions must data[p / 8] shift right to bring the requested bit to bit 0?
questions.hint: Within-byte stream offset is p % 8; reading is MSB first.
questions.explanation: The offset is 3, so the shift is 7 − 3 = 4.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Number the eight bits of data[0] from its MSB to its LSB, then continue the same way through data[1], data[2], and so on, beginning at global position 0. For p = 8, what right-shift count brings that stream bit to bit 0?
questions.hint: Position 8 begins a new byte.
questions.explanation: p % 8 is 0; the first stream bit in a byte is its most significant bit, so shift by 7.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Number the eight bits of data[0] from its MSB to its LSB, then continue the same way through data[1], data[2], and so on, beginning at global position 0. Write an expression that yields 0 or 1 for global bit p in unsigned-char buffer data. Assume p is valid.
questions.hint: Select the byte, shift the desired bit down, then isolate it.
questions.explanation: p / 8 chooses the byte. MSB-first indexing gives shift 7 − p % 8. & 1u removes every other bit.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
rubric: Uses p / 8 to select the byte.
Uses 7 − p % 8 for the shift.
Masks with 1 to produce exactly 0 or 1.

questions.prompt: What bit value does this expression yield?
questions.hint: p = 7 selects the last bit of the first byte.
questions.explanation: 0x81 is binary 10000001. Position 7 uses shift 0; masking its low bit produces 1.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Number the eight bits of data[0] from its MSB to its LSB, then continue the same way through data[1], data[2], and so on, beginning at global position 0. For data = {0x80, 0x01}, what is the value of global bit 8?
questions.hint: Global bit 8 is the MSB of data[1].
questions.explanation: data[1] is 00000001, whose most significant bit is 0. Its one-bit is at global position 15.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Number the eight bits of data[0] from its MSB to its LSB, then continue the same way through data[1], data[2], and so on, beginning at global position 0. For data = {0x80, 0x01}, what is the value of global bit 15?
questions.hint: Global bit 15 is the final bit of the second byte.
questions.explanation: 15 / 8 = 1 and 7 − 15 % 8 = 0. The low bit of 0x01 is 1.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: An array contains 5 eight-bit bytes. Number all its bits consecutively starting at zero. What is the last valid global bit position?
questions.hint: Positions begin at zero.
questions.explanation: There are 8 × 5 = 40 bits, so positions run from 0 through 39.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: An array contains 2 eight-bit bytes. Number all its bits consecutively starting at zero. What is the first out-of-range global bit position?
questions.hint: The first invalid position equals the bit count.
questions.explanation: Two bytes contain 16 bits at positions 0 through 15. Position 16 would be outside this array.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: The next bit b is 0 or 1. Write the update that appends b on the right of unsigned int accumulator value. Assume a one-place left shift loses no set bits.
questions.hint: Make one low-bit space before inserting b.
questions.explanation: Left shift moves the existing bits up one place; OR inserts b at the new least significant position. Addition of b is also equivalent here.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.
rubric: Shifts the previous value left by one.
Inserts b in the vacated low position.

questions.prompt: value is 5 and the next bit b is 1. What is the new value after `(value << 1) | b`?
questions.hint: Old binary 101 becomes 1011.
questions.explanation: The update is 2 × 5 + 1 = 11. It preserves the order of bits encountered.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Starting from zero, accumulate bits 1, 0, 1, 1 in that order using left-shift-and-append. What decimal value results?
questions.hint: The first received bit becomes the most significant bit of this four-bit field.
questions.explanation: The intermediate values are 1, 2, 5, 11. Do not reverse the received bit order.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: Starting from unsigned value = 0, process bits 0, 1, 0, 0, 0 in that order, updating value = (value << 1) | bit each time. What final decimal value results?
questions.hint: Accumulate the explicitly listed bits as the binary number 01000.
questions.explanation: The accumulator evolves 0, 1, 2, 4, 8. Appending a bit multiplies the old value by two and adds that bit.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: data is {0x12, 0x34}. Number bits from zero, starting at data[0]’s MSB and continuing MSB first through data[1]. Read 8 bits beginning at position 4, interpreting the first selected bit as most significant. What unsigned decimal value results?
questions.hint: Join the low four bits of 0x12 to the high four bits of 0x34.
questions.explanation: The selected bits are 0010 0011, which is 0x23 = 35. The field crosses a byte boundary without resetting its accumulator.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: data is {0xab, 0xcd}. Number bits from zero, starting at data[0]’s MSB and continuing MSB first through data[1]. Read 6 bits beginning at position 6, interpreting the first selected bit as most significant. What unsigned decimal value results?
questions.hint: Take the last two bits of 0xab, then the first four bits of 0xcd.
questions.explanation: The selected bits are 11 followed by 1100: 111100 = 60.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: What is the value of pos after this code?
questions.hint: The increment is given directly by the code.
questions.explanation: pos advances by 3, from 13 to 16. A cursor advances by the number of positions actually consumed; no unstated alignment is implied.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: What is the final value of pos after this code?
questions.hint: Add each consumed width exactly once.
questions.explanation: The two increments are 3 and 9. The final cursor is 6 + 3 + 9 = 18.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: What is the largest unsigned integer representable using 4 bits?
questions.hint: All four raw bits can be one before signed interpretation.
questions.explanation: The four-bit pattern 1111 has unsigned value 2^4 − 1 = 15. Interpreting the same pattern as signed would be a different operation.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: What is the largest unsigned raw value obtainable from 31 bits?
questions.hint: Compute 2^31 − 1.
questions.explanation: The maximum is 2^31 − 1 = 2147483647. A 32-bit unsigned int can hold every unsigned value extracted from at most 31 bits.
questions.source: C17 integer and bitwise expressions; WG14 N1570 §§6.3.1.1, 6.5.7, 6.5.10–6.5.12. Any bit-reading order is specified in this exercise.

questions.prompt: A six-bit two’s-complement integer is stored in the low 6 bits of unsigned int raw. What bit index contains its sign bit? Number bits from zero at the least significant bit.
questions.hint: The highest of L bits has index L − 1.
questions.explanation: The sign bit is bit 5 of this six-bit raw field, not bit 31 of its storage type.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: The low L bits of unsigned int raw hold an L-bit two’s-complement integer, with 1 <= L <= 31. Write an unsigned expression that tests whether this represented integer is negative. Number bits from zero at the least significant bit.
questions.hint: The payload’s own most significant bit carries its sign.
questions.explanation: A shifted-and-masked alternative is also valid. Test bit L − 1 rather than the storage type’s top bit.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.
rubric: Selects bit L − 1.
Distinguishes zero from a set sign bit.
Uses a safe shift for the stated L range.

questions.prompt: Interpret the four-bit pattern 1101 as a two’s-complement integer. Its unsigned raw value is 13. What signed value does it represent?
questions.hint: With its sign bit set, subtract 2^L.
questions.explanation: The highest of the four bits is set, so the signed value is 13 − 2^4 = −3.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: Interpret the five-bit pattern 11111 as a two’s-complement integer. Its unsigned raw value is 31. What signed value does it represent?
questions.hint: Subtract the modulus for this payload width.
questions.explanation: 31 − 32 = −1. All ones encodes −1 at every nonzero two’s-complement width.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: Interpret the four-bit pattern 0000 as a two’s-complement integer. What signed value does it represent?
questions.hint: A zero sign bit means nonnegative, not strictly positive.
questions.explanation: The sign bit is clear and every value bit is zero, so the represented integer is zero. A clear sign bit means nonnegative, not strictly positive.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: Interpret the five-bit pattern 01111 as a two’s-complement integer. Its unsigned raw value is 15. What signed value does it represent?
questions.hint: Only the highest of these five bits determines negativity.
questions.explanation: The sign bit at index 4 is zero, so the signed value remains 15.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum value representable by a five-bit two’s-complement integer?
questions.hint: An L-bit signed range begins at −2^(L−1).
questions.explanation: The minimum bit pattern is 10000, raw 16. Subtracting 32 gives −16.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum value representable by a 31-bit two’s-complement integer?
questions.hint: Use the payload width, not the 32-bit storage width.
questions.explanation: The minimum is −2^30 = −1073741824. The signed range has one more negative value than positive value.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: Interpret the one-bit pattern 1 as a two’s-complement integer. What signed value does it represent?
questions.hint: Its only bit is also its sign bit.
questions.explanation: raw = 1 and L = 1, so 1 − 2 = −1. A one-bit signed field cannot encode positive 1.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: What is the largest signed value representable by a one-bit two’s-complement integer?
questions.hint: The two available patterns encode zero and negative one.
questions.explanation: Pattern 0 encodes 0 and pattern 1 encodes −1; therefore the maximum is 0.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: The low L bits of unsigned int raw represent a negative L-bit two’s-complement integer, with 1 <= L <= 31 and no higher bits set. Repair this int-returning function’s negative branch so the arithmetic is defined even at L = 31.
questions.hint: Do the power of two and subtraction in a signed type wide enough for 2^31.
questions.explanation: 1 << 31 is invalid for signed 32-bit int. long long safely holds raw, 2^L and their difference; the final result fits int under these assumptions.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.
questions.code:
/* sign bit is known to be set */
return (int)raw - (1 << L);
rubric: Uses a type wide enough for 2^31, such as long long.
Subtracts 2^L from raw with signed wide arithmetic.
Produces the signed int result without relying on an out-of-range unsigned-to-int conversion.

questions.prompt: An int-returning function must interpret the low L bits of unsigned int raw as a negative L-bit two’s-complement integer. Assume 1 <= L <= 31 and no higher bits set. Why is `return raw - (1u << L);` not a portable negative-value calculation in C17? Give a safe expression.
questions.answer: The subtraction is unsigned, so a negative mathematical answer wraps to a large unsigned value; converting that out-of-range value to int is implementation-defined in C17. Use (int)((long long)raw - (1LL << L)).
questions.hint: Changing the shift operand to unsigned also changes the subtraction’s arithmetic type.
questions.explanation: An unsigned mask is useful for bit tests. Signed interpretation needs arithmetic whose negative result is representable before the final conversion.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.
rubric: Identifies unsigned subtraction and wraparound.
Avoids assuming out-of-range unsigned-to-int conversion is portable.
Gives a safe wider signed subtraction.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum value representable by a 31-bit two’s-complement integer?
questions.hint: The sign bit must stay zero; the other 30 bits may all be one.
questions.explanation: The maximum is 2^30 − 1 = 1073741823. Of the 31 bits, the sign bit is zero and the remaining 30 bits are ones.
questions.source: Two’s-complement representation and C17 integer conversions under the stated practice assumptions; WG14 N1570 §§6.2.6.2, 6.3.1.3, 6.5.7.

questions.prompt: How many times is steps incremented?
questions.hint: Trace pos at the start of each loop iteration.
questions.explanation: The loop body runs at pos = 0, 2, 4 and 6. It stops after pos becomes 8, so steps is 4.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.

questions.prompt: How many times is count incremented?
questions.hint: Check the condition before entering the loop body.
questions.explanation: The initial remainder is 12 − 7 = 5, which is less than the required 6 in this code. The loop body never executes.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.

questions.prompt: size_t pos is a cursor into totalBits bits, and pos <= totalBits. Write a condition that checks whether width further bits fit, without risking overflow in pos + width.
questions.hint: Use the remaining count rather than unchecked addition.
questions.explanation: Since pos <= totalBits, the subtraction is safe. Comparing width with the remaining count avoids overflowing a sum such as pos + width.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.
rubric: Compares width with totalBits − pos.
Uses the stated pos <= totalBits precondition.

questions.prompt: An array has 16 valid elements, indexed from zero, and its next unread element is at index 10. How many valid elements remain from that index onward?
questions.hint: Subtract the next unread index from the element count.
questions.explanation: The remaining count is 16 − 10 = 6. A request to read 7 elements starting there would exceed the array’s valid range.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.

questions.prompt: What is the final value of pos?
questions.hint: Each statement advances the same variable.
questions.explanation: The final value is 7 + 3 + 4 = 14. Do not infer extra increments that are absent from the code.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.

questions.prompt: This function receives a pointer to the caller’s cursor. What value does pos have after the call?
questions.hint: *cursor designates the caller’s size_t object.
questions.explanation: The function adds 3 directly to the caller’s pos through its pointer. pos changes from 12 to 15.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.

questions.prompt: What is count after this loop?
questions.hint: The break happens before the increment on the zero element.
questions.explanation: The element 3 increments count once. At the next element, 0, break exits the loop before another increment.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.

questions.prompt: What is count after this loop?
questions.hint: This version increments before checking the stop condition.
questions.explanation: The loop increments count for 3 and then for 0. It then breaks, leaving count at 2. Moving a statement across a break condition can change the result.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.

questions.prompt: What is final after both outer-loop iterations?
questions.hint: count is declared and initialized again inside each outer iteration.
questions.explanation: count becomes 1 separately during each iteration because it is reset to zero inside the outer loop. The last assignment stores 1 in final.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.

questions.prompt: What is count after this code?
questions.hint: This time count is initialized outside the loop.
questions.explanation: Both increments affect the same count without reinitializing it. Its final value is 2.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in result?
questions.hint: First shift the byte right, then keep its low three bits.
questions.explanation: 0xb6 is 10110110. Shifting right by 3 gives 00010110; AND with 00000111 leaves 00000110 = 6.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.
questions.code:
unsigned char byte = 0xb6;
unsigned int result = (byte >> 3) & 7u;

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in result?
questions.hint: Isolate the four bits selected by the shift and mask.
questions.explanation: 0xd6 is 11010110. Its high four bits are 1101, so the result is 13.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.
questions.code:
unsigned char byte = 0xd6;
unsigned int result = (byte >> 4) & 15u;

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in value?
questions.hint: Compute raw first, then apply the conditional subtraction.
questions.explanation: raw is 0xd = 13. raw & 8u is nonzero, so value is 13 − 16 = −3. The code interprets the selected four bits as two’s complement.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in value?
questions.hint: The mask selects five bits; the sign test checks the bit of weight 16.
questions.explanation: raw is 0x1a = 26. Its bit 4 is set, so the conditional computes 26 − 32 = −6.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in raw?
questions.hint: The low four bits of data[0] become the high four bits of the result.
questions.explanation: data[0] & 15u is 2, shifted left four gives 32. data[1] >> 4 is 3. Their OR is 35, the value 0x23.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.
questions.code:
unsigned char data[] = {0x12, 0x34};
unsigned int raw = ((data[0] & 15u) << 4) | (data[1] >> 4);

questions.prompt: What decimal value is stored in raw?
questions.hint: The low two bits of the first byte are joined to the high four bits of the second byte.
questions.explanation: data[0] & 3u is 3, shifted left four gives 48. data[1] >> 4 is 12. The OR is 60, binary 111100.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.
questions.code:
unsigned char data[] = {0xab, 0xcd};
unsigned int raw = ((data[0] & 3u) << 4) | (data[1] >> 4);

questions.prompt: After this code, give the decimal values of data[0], data[1], and x.
questions.hint: The increment moves p before the write, and x is computed from that updated byte.
questions.explanation: p starts at data[0], then ++p makes it point to data[1]. OR with 4 changes 0x20 to 0x24 = 36. Shifting 36 right by 2 gives x = 9.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.
rubric: Leaves data[0] at 16.
Changes data[1] to 36.
Computes x as 9 after the change.

questions.prompt: A program allocates 16 bytes, then successfully receives 2 bytes of input into that storage. It should process only the received input. How many bits may it process: 128 or 16? Explain.
questions.answer: 16 bits. The valid input length is 2 bytes × 8 bits per byte; the extra allocated capacity is not additional input.
questions.hint: Storage space and valid input length are different quantities.
questions.explanation: Capacity and valid input length are distinct values. Spare allocation does not establish that those bytes belong to the input.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.
rubric: Uses 2 × 8 = 16 valid bits.
Distinguishes storage capacity from received input length.

questions.prompt: A 10-byte allocation contains exactly 3 received input bytes; only those bytes may be processed. Number their bits consecutively from zero. What is the first global position outside that received input?
questions.hint: Use received bytes, not allocated capacity, to set the stream boundary.
questions.explanation: The input contains 3 × 8 = 24 bits at positions 0 through 23. Its first out-of-range position is 24; extra storage capacity does not extend that input.
questions.source: C17 language concepts; WG14 N1570: integer types, conversions, expressions and standard-library contracts.

questions.prompt: Write getBit from memory. Contract: data is a valid byte array and p is a valid zero-based global bit position. Number bits starting at data[0]’s MSB, continue to its LSB, then continue the same way through later bytes. Return exactly 0 or 1 for position p.
questions.hint: Recall the three steps: select byte, move bit, isolate bit.
questions.explanation: Divide p by 8 to select a byte. The given MSB-first convention makes the shift 7 − p % 8. The caller guarantees p is in range.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.
rubric: Uses the requested signature and returns 0 or 1.
Selects data[p / 8].
Shifts by 7 − p % 8 and masks one bit.

questions.prompt: Write getBitChecked. Number bits from zero, starting at data[0]’s MSB, continuing to its LSB and then through subsequent bytes in the same order. The valid input has B bytes. Return 1 and store the bit in *out when p is valid; otherwise return 0 and leave *out unchanged. data and out are valid for their uses, and B <= SIZE_MAX / 8.
questions.hint: Check the position before touching data or the output.
questions.explanation: The boundary is exclusive: p equal to the bit count is already invalid. Checking p / 8 >= B is another valid approach that avoids multiplication.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.
rubric: Rejects all out-of-range positions before reading.
Leaves *out unchanged on failure.
Stores the correctly extracted 0/1 bit and returns 1 on success.

questions.prompt: Write getBits using the supplied helper `unsigned int getBit(const unsigned char *data, size_t p)`. getBit returns 0 or 1 for global position p, counting from zero through each byte MSB first in array order. Read k bits starting at p, with the first read bit becoming the result’s most significant bit. Assume 0 <= k <= 31 and all requested positions are valid. Return 0 for k = 0.
questions.hint: Initialize, repeat exactly k times, append the next bit.
questions.explanation: Start the result at zero and append each bit by shifting left once and inserting the new low bit. The requested width never exceeds 31, so all intermediate values fit unsigned int.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.
rubric: Initializes the accumulator to zero.
Consumes exactly p through p + k − 1 in order.
Uses left-shift-and-append and returns the accumulator.
Handles k = 0 without reading a bit.

questions.prompt: Write readField using `unsigned int getBits(const unsigned char *data, size_t p, unsigned int k)`. getBits returns the next k bits starting at zero-based position p, reading each byte MSB first in array order and treating the first selected bit as most significant; it returns 0 for k = 0 and does no bounds checks. readField must return 1 and write *out only when k <= 31 and the full range [p, p+k) fits in totalBits. Otherwise return 0 and leave *out unchanged. All pointers are valid for their uses; data contains totalBits valid bits.
questions.hint: Check p before subtracting it; do not rely on p + k staying in range.
questions.explanation: The ordered bounds checks prevent unsigned subtraction underflow and addition overflow. A zero-length field at p == totalBits is permitted by this helper’s contract.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.
rubric: Rejects k > 31 and p > totalBits.
Checks remaining capacity without unsafe subtraction or addition.
Only writes *out on success.
Accepts a valid zero-bit request and returns zero through *out.

questions.prompt: Write decodeSigned. The low L bits of unsigned int raw contain an L-bit two’s-complement integer; no higher bits are set and 1 <= L <= 31. Return that represented signed value as int, without undefined shifts or out-of-range unsigned-to-int conversion.
questions.hint: Test bit L − 1, then subtract 2^L in a sufficiently wide signed type if set.
questions.explanation: Test bit L − 1. A clear sign bit leaves raw unchanged; a set sign bit requires subtracting 2^L in a sufficiently wide signed type. Both resulting branches fit int.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.
rubric: Tests the payload sign bit at L − 1.
Keeps nonnegative raw values unchanged.
Computes raw − 2^L safely for the negative branch, including L = 31.

questions.prompt: Write readByte. Read one hex integer from stdin. Return 1 and store it in *out only if conversion succeeds and its value is at most 255; otherwise return 0 and leave *out unchanged. Assume the token, if numeric, fits unsigned int.
questions.hint: Match scanf’s destination type before checking the byte range.
questions.explanation: A conversion check prevents use of an unassigned temporary. The range check prevents accepting a value that would be truncated to fit one byte.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.
rubric: Uses unsigned int temporary and %x with its address.
Checks both conversion success and the byte range.
Writes through out only after both checks and returns the specified status.

questions.prompt: Write nextValue using the two supplied helpers. getBits(data, p, k) returns k bits starting at zero-based position p, reading bytes in array order and bits MSB first, with the first selected bit most significant; it performs no bounds checks. decodeSigned(raw, width) returns the two’s-complement value of the low width bits. nextValue must read exactly width bits at *pos and update *out and *pos only on success. Return -1 for width outside 1..31 or *pos > totalBits; return 0 when a valid cursor equals totalBits; return -1 when too few bits remain; otherwise return 1. Check these conditions in the stated order. All pointers are valid for their uses, and data contains totalBits valid bits.
questions.hint: Validate the width and cursor before subtraction. Keep changes local until every check passes.
questions.explanation: A capacity check against totalBits − start ensures the read and later cursor addition fit. Returning early preserves both output objects when the function does not successfully read a value.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.
rubric: Rejects invalid widths or an invalid cursor before reading.
Returns 0 for a valid end cursor, before testing the remaining field size.
Rejects a field wider than totalBits − *pos without unsigned underflow.
On success reads width bits, interprets them using decodeSigned, and advances by width.
Leaves *pos and *out unchanged on all non-success paths.

questions.prompt: Write lowMask. Contract: 0 <= k <= 31. Return an unsigned int whose low k bits are 1 and remaining bits are 0. Do not loop; support k = 0.
questions.hint: A one at bit k minus one fills every lower bit.
questions.explanation: For k = 0 the expression is 1 − 1 = 0. For k = 31 the unsigned shift is valid. Extending this unchanged to k = 32 would violate the shift-count rule.
questions.source: C17 arrays, integer arithmetic and functions; the complete exercise contract is stated in the prompt.
rubric: Uses unsigned arithmetic.
Produces exactly the low k one-bits.
Returns zero for k = 0 and remains defined at k = 31.
